PART NINE
Decisions & the Future
CHAPTER 79
Facing a Major Decision
The two options are still there after another evening of
thinking. One offers something you want and asks you to give up
something you value. The other protects what is familiar but has
costs of its own. You may be looking for a sign that would
remove the possibility of choosing badly.
A significant decision can remain difficult even after you have
considered it responsibly. Different good things may be in
tension, and some consequences cannot be known in advance.
Wisdom helps you attend to the choice you actually have,
including the people it affects.
Begin by stating what needs deciding and when. “Should I
change my life?” is too large to examine usefully. “Should I
accept this offer by Friday?” allows you to identify what
information is missing and whose circumstances need
consideration. Be careful about accepting an artificial deadline
from someone who benefits if you decide before asking
questions.

375
Solomon asks about the people he must govern
In 1 Kings 3, the Lord appears to Solomon in a dream and invites
him to ask for what he wants. Solomon speaks about the
responsibility of succeeding David as king. He describes himself
as a little child who does not know how to carry out the task. He
asks for an understanding heart to govern God's people and
distinguish good from evil.
The Lord is pleased with the request and grants him wisdom.
The account concerns a king's calling and a particular response
from God. Its attention to the people Solomon will govern is
useful for anyone considering a decision with effects beyond
themselves.
You might want to know which option will make you happiest
or appear most successful. Include those hopes in your thinking,
then consider who else will live with the result. A decision about
work may affect a partner's responsibilities or a child's care. An
undertaking at church may depend on time someone else will
have to supply. Their lives deserve a place in the conversation.
You can ask God for the capacity to judge well before asking Him
to confirm your preferred option. James writes:
Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives
generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to
him.
James 1:5, Berean Standard Bible
The surrounding passage concerns perseverance in trials and
wholehearted reliance on God. Asking for wisdom belongs in a
life of trust. It does not require you to report perfect confidence
about a particular job or move before asking for help.

376
Put the facts beside the hopes
Consider what you know about each option. Which benefits are
established, and which depend on someone else's assurance?
What commitments would you make? What would happen if
the hoped-for benefit did not arrive?
If the choice involves money, healthcare, or a legal
commitment, obtain advice suited to that matter. A trusted
friend may know your character well while having little
knowledge of the agreement you are considering. Spiritual
counsel and professional information can contribute different
things.
There may be an option you have not considered because the
decision has been presented as a choice between two extremes.
Ask whether the terms can be clarified or whether a smaller
commitment is possible. You may discover room to change the
proposal, or learn why the available choice is narrower than you
hoped.
Examine the moral questions plainly. A gain that depends on
deception or neglecting a responsibility needs more than a
favorable comparison of advantages. For a Christian, love of God
and neighbor belongs within the decision, including how the
choice will be carried out.
Sometimes both options allow a faithful life. One might provide
more time with family while another makes work you value
possible. Ask which responsibility carries greater weight in your
present circumstances. You may have to accept the loss of one
good thing in choosing another. That loss deserves
acknowledgment, even when the choice is sound.

377
Hear advice without handing over the decision
Choose someone able to listen to the facts and challenge your
preferred account. Tell them what draws you to an option and
what you would rather avoid mentioning. Ask which
assumption they think needs checking.
Advice can be sincere and still reflect the adviser's preferences.
Someone may favor security, adventure, or closeness to family
more strongly than you do. Hear their reasons and consider
their knowledge of your circumstances. Their certainty does not
relieve you of your responsibility to judge.
Your feelings are worth noticing too. Unease may identify a
concern that needs investigation. Relief may come from a good
decision, or simply from ending a difficult discussion. Neither
feeling, taken alone, establishes God's instruction. Pray,
examine the reasons, and allow your emotions to be part of the
information you consider.
Choose with an honest account of the limits
Once the relevant information and counsel are available,
identify the reasons you can stand behind. You may still have
uncertainty. Make the decision with that uncertainty
acknowledged and attend to the commitments it creates.
Where a review will be possible, decide what would make one
useful. A later difficulty does not automatically prove that the
original choice was wrong. New information may also justify
changing course. You can remain accountable without requiring
a single decision to settle the whole of your future.
If someone you care about faces a major decision
Ask whether they want help gathering information, a place to
talk, or your view. If you offer an opinion, make your reasons
clear and disclose any interest you have in the outcome.

378
Avoid presenting your preference as a message from God that
they must obey. Respect their right to decide, while speaking
honestly about a serious risk. When a decision will directly
affect you, explain your own needs and responsibilities as part of
the discussion.
For reflection
• What exactly needs deciding, and what is the real deadline?
• Which assumption most needs checking before you commit?
• Who will be affected, and have their circumstances been
heard?
Prayer
God, give me wisdom for this decision. Help me see the facts clearly
and be honest about what I want. Keep me attentive to those
affected. Guide me toward useful counsel, and help me take
responsibility for my choice even when I cannot foresee every
consequence. Amen.
For further reading: 1 Kings 3:5–15; James 1:2–8; Proverbs 3:5–7; Proverbs 15:22; 2
Chronicles 20:10–17.
Read also: Facing a Major Financial Decision (p. 148), Living with an Uncertain Future
(p. 379), When Change Frightens You (p. 397).
